Three things. The first reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a saying to be studied - an order to be obeyed. The one we remember as first among us heard those words read aloud in church and took them as meant for him alone. Before the day ended he had begun giving everything away. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than an argument about who he was: a direct word demanding a total response, all at once.

The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we did not think this rested on our say-so. Read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation.

The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it rose. The knowledge of God spread. And death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. That is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer asked of us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. His coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man. It is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe in him.

One of us taught it this way: let us hold on to our discipline, let us not grow careless, for in it the Lord is our fellow-worker - to die daily, as the apostle put it, and so not sin, treating every day as though it might be the last one given to us. Following him meant following him into that.

The same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. We did not have a separate collection or a private Gospel preserved only among us. What reached us was what had reached everyone: the writings the church already held as Scripture by the time our own formation began. We were not the ones who decided what belonged in that collection. That happened before us, elsewhere, among those who held that kind of authority.

How those writings first traveled from their own making to the church that held them when we began - that chain of transmission happened before our own time started, and we were not the ones carrying it. We can tell you where we stood in relation to it: we received what the wider church had already received, and we used it differently than most did, not as a different collection. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for one struggle at a time, rather than studying it whole or arguing over it line by line. 

One of us heard a passage read aloud - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - and took it as though it had been spoken to him alone. That is how Scripture worked among us: not as a text to be mastered, but as a word that could find you where you stood.

We cannot give you a story of someone among us who doubted and then came to believe - the kind of account you might be hoping to hear. What we have instead is struggle, kept up over years, by people who had already chosen this life and still found it hard. Moses wrestled with old habits for a long time after he came to us. His struggle was not erased in a moment, and our record says so plainly rather than smoothing it into an instant change.

Another of us heard one command as though it were spoken straight to him: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. He took it as his own call and obeyed it. Even then, his own withdrawal deepened over years - each time solitude drew a crowd, he went further. It was not one moment of certainty that held him. It was a life lived as though the command were true, tested again and again.

We cannot promise you a sudden feeling. What we can tell you is that staying in the struggle, without forcing a certainty you do not have, was itself how belief was held among us. One of our own teachers put it plainly: God sometimes puts into us the very beginnings of salvation, and gives a person the zeal of his own will. The start may not be yours to control. What you do with it once it arrives - that part is yours. We lived by discernment, diakrisis - the skill of judging rightly what a person can actually bear. Not everyone was given the same discipline, because not everyone could carry it. If you cannot yet believe, we would not tell you to pretend. We would tell you to live as though it mattered whether you could, and see what becomes possible.

We held, when it mattered, that the Son of God was not some lesser, created thing brought into being out of nothing, but the Eternal Word of the Father's own being. There was never a time when he was not. That is what one of us stood up in Alexandria to say, when the bishops summoned him down from his own mountain to answer the Arians publicly. 

The reason we gave for why he came was this: the Word of God took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. He was not changed into something lesser. He remained what he was, and took on what we are. The proof, we said to those who doubted, was not argument but power: read the accounts and see that the deeds of Christ - the dead raised, the blind given sight, the walking on the sea - prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation.

About the Spirit: there was another current among us that spoke of this more directly. The soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye. The Spirit of the Lord makes himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight - known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. That voice held the three together without working out how they fit as a system. It spoke from what was actually felt, not from what could be argued.

We did not sit in council and work out how Father, Son, and Spirit relate to each other as a matter of doctrine. The bishops did that work. What we did was refuse communion with anyone who taught that the Son was a created thing. That was our boundary, and we kept it.

We did not spend our days working out God's own nature the way a theologian in the city might have. Most of us were formed to see him, not to argue about him. But when it mattered, we said what we held plainly enough that you can know where we stood.

The Son of God is not some lesser, created thing, not brought into being out of nothing, but the Eternal Word of the Father's own being. There was never a time when he was not. When the Arians claimed one of us as agreeing with them, the bishops sent for him - he came down from his own mountain to the city, stood up in public, denounced them, and taught what the settled faith actually held. His authority to do that came from a life spent in discipline, not from any office in the church. And when our own founder was pressed by visiting philosophers to defend what we held, he said it this way: the Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason he came at all.

Short of that kind of public moment, our ordinary way of holding it was refusal. We would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise. Beyond that boundary, the deepest of us - and only a few went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind. Strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. The most systematic among us called that contemplation - theoria, his word for it. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

We did not settle it ourselves, and we did not pretend otherwise. The councils that decided what the church would hold were run by bishops, in the cities, not by us. But we were not silent either. Once, the Arians claimed one of us as agreeing with them. The bishops sent for him. He came down from his own mountain to the city, stood up in public, denounced the Arians, and taught what the settled faith actually held. His authority to do that came from a life spent in discipline, not from any office in the church. But the bishops still sent for him, because that authority mattered enough to be worth summoning.

What we can tell you about the process itself is this much: the desert elder came when called, spoke plainly to refute the contested position, and pointed to the deeds of Christ as proof - the dead raised, the blind seeing, paralytics healed, lepers cleansed, the walking on water. Those signs, he said, show that Christ is no longer a man, but God. That is what we have: one elder summoned, one public refusal of the Arian position, and the weight his own earned authority carried when he gave it. We do not have a wider pattern showing how often this happened, or whether other settlements handled disputed questions the same way. The authority tension we never resolved - whether real weight belonged to a person's own earned discernment or to an office under a Rule - runs through the whole of this material structurally, but no single dramatized scene of someone navigating that tension directly has been identified in what survives. We are telling you what we actually have, not inventing the rest to fill the silence.

We were not a place of confessed doubt - that is the first honest thing to tell you. No saying and no story of ours shows someone among us standing up to say plainly, I cannot believe, and being answered in those words. What we have instead is the record of struggle kept up over years by people who had already chosen this life and still found it hard.

One of us went to hear the Gospel read and took it as spoken straight to him: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow. He gave away most of what he owned that same day - but not all of it. It took a second hearing, some time later, before he gave the rest. Even for him, following did not happen all at once. Another of us, much later, prayed twice for a way forward - the first answer sent him to Egypt, the second gave him the three words that stayed with him: flee, be silent, be still. The answer came at the far end of a struggle already under way, not handed to him at the start.

The longer struggle was against the thoughts that pulled a person's mind away - logismoi, we called them. One of our teachers worked out a whole system for naming and answering them, but most of us fought without that kind of map. What we held in common was this: the thought arriving is not your failure. You do not control the knock at the door. You decide whether it moves in. Watchfulness - nepsis, our word for it - meant learning to catch a thought early, while it was still small. And one of us walked to a gathering carrying a jug with a hole in it, water running out behind him the whole way. When they asked him why, he said: my own sins run out behind me, and I do not see them - and yet I come to judge another man's.

If you are asking whether we had a place for someone still finding their way toward belief, rather than someone defending what they already held - our record does not give us that story in so many words. What it gives us is people who chose the discipline and still wrestled with it for years. We cannot promise you a sudden certainty. We can tell you that staying in the struggle, without forcing a feeling you did not have, was how the life was actually lived among us.

Were people born already guilty, carrying Adam's sin? We have no answer to give - no letter and no story of ours speaks to it in so many words.

What we did argue at length was whether a person is saved by effort alone or by grace. The question was put to us directly: if someone strives with all his might for a good result, can he become master of what is good? The answer that started the argument was no - not unless he has it as a gift. We thought grace and free will looked opposed to each other, but really were in harmony; we ought to have both alike. What we would say plainly is this: the main share in our salvation belongs not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace. Sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation, and gives a person the zeal of his own will. Sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work. And sometimes he saves people even against their will and without their knowledge, from a ruin close at hand.

Someone asked one of our elders what happens to a person who dies still at war, with both sin and grace in the same soul at once. The answer did not weigh the two. He goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. That the war comes upon you is not your doing. But to hate it - that is yours.

We did not read Scripture the way a scholar does, and we did not leave behind commentaries explaining it line by line. What we did instead was take it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. An elder would answer a question not with his own opinion but with a line of Scripture - the words themselves carried the weight.

The Psalter we knew by heart, returned to constantly. And a smaller circle among us went further still. They gathered verses into a weapon - antirrhesis, we called it - to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose. Not a commentary explaining the passage, but the text itself turned into a tool for the immediate fight. Even there it stayed applied: answering a struggle, not interpreting a text.

One of our teachers arranged it this way: the three books of Solomon correspond to the three kinds of renunciation we practice. Proverbs teaches the first renunciation - putting away bodily sin and training the character. Ecclesiastes teaches the second - seeing through the world's own emptiness. The Song of Songs belongs to the third and highest - the soul's contemplation of heavenly things. That is how we read: not to explain what the words once meant in their own time, but to meet the struggle we were in right then.

We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else. That was the purpose.

Looking at our own record honestly, most of what we say would survive scrutiny - but the scrutiny would also force us to name our limits more clearly than we sometimes do.

What would stand:

The basic shape of our life - withdrawal, manual labor, struggle against tempting thoughts, elder-mediated teaching, discernment as master virtue - all of that rests on substantial, converging evidence.

The three organizational patterns existing at once - solitary anchorites, Pachomian federation, semi-anchoritic settlements - documented and distinct.

The sayings themselves, as a real teaching form, even though they reach us through later compilation.

The basic content of what we held about Christ - the Nicene formulation, his death as already having defeated what we fight, following him as total giving - all directly attested.

Where scrutiny would demand more honesty from us:

Our single-voice problem is worse than we always admit. Antony's portrait depends overwhelmingly on one bishop's construction, and whether Antony was actually unlettered or more philosophically formed than that portrait allows is genuinely contested. We should state that uncertainty more plainly every time we speak of him, not just when directly asked.

The compiler mediation is real throughout. We sometimes speak as though we know how a saying was delivered or how often a pattern recurred, when actually we know it only through later editorial arrangement. A scholar would catch us overstating there.

The women's material is thinner than our carefully hedged language sometimes suggests. We have named women, reported speech inside third-person narration, and a handful of attributed sayings. What we do not have is a woman speaking at length in her own person - and the narrated women arrive at chapter thirty-five, after thirty-four chapters of men, in a section the compiler has to announce before he writes it. That structural fact says something about how central women were in the tradition's own memory, and we should state it more plainly.

The Melitian question: we refuse them communion, but their own documentary archive shows ordinary ascetic business that looks similar to ours. Whether that similarity is real or an artifact of limited evidence is genuinely open, and we should keep saying so.

The authority tension is structurally visible but never dramatized in a single preserved scene showing someone navigating it directly. We state that limit in our cautions, but we could be more consistent about it in conversation.

Where we are actually strongest:

On the core practice of discernment, spiritual combat, and what the fight against thoughts actually looked like day to day - here the sayings, the systematic teaching, and the founding narrative all converge, and a scholar would find the evidence thick.

On the economic embeddedness - archaeological and documentary evidence corroborates a working, trade-connected life alongside the withdrawal rhetoric.

On our honest limits themselves - we do not invent to fill gaps. A scholar might wish we had more material, but would not catch us claiming what we do not have.

The hardest question a scholar would press us on: are we sometimes too confident about generalizing from one or two voices to the whole movement? Yes. We should be more careful about that.

We do not know, in the way you are asking. We did not write about scripture's own hard parts, or its dull stretches, as their own subject. We used the parts that spoke to one struggle at a time. We did not dwell on the rest.

What we can tell you is how we did use it, and what we thought it was for. Most of us did not argue about God for a living. We were formed to see him. Scripture was the tool that shaped that seeing. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own. The words themselves carried the weight. A smaller circle among us went further, collecting verses into a weapon to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose - not a commentary explaining the text, but the text itself turned into a tool for the fight.

One of us put the whole life into a pattern drawn from Scripture's own shape. He said the three books of Solomon correspond to three kinds of renunciation. Proverbs teaches the first: giving up the confusion of ordinary village life. Ecclesiastes teaches the second: seeing through every visible thing to its vanity, so the soul no longer clings. The Song of Songs teaches the third: the soul drawn up into contemplation of heavenly things, held by nothing in this world. That is Scripture used as a map of the whole ascent, not as a book to be explained.

We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else. That may not be what you are asking for. It is what we actually have to give you.

We held Scripture as our one written authority - nothing of our own alongside it. But authority itself came to us two different ways, and we never settled which one really governed the other.

In the solitary and semi-solitary patterns, authority was earned through a lifetime of discernment - diakrisis, our word for the skill of judging rightly between thoughts and practices - and it traveled through the elder's own person, not through any office. A saying, an apophthegma, carried weight because the elder who spoke it had proven himself through discipline, not because he held a title. You came to him with one struggle, he gave you one word fitted to that moment, and the authority was in the relationship itself.

In the cenobitic pattern - Pachomius's linked houses, the Koinonia - authority came through a written Rule and appointed offices: housemaster, steward, positions held by assignment rather than by a life's own witness. That Rule itself was said to have come from an angel, handed to Pachomius on a tablet of iron. It governed thousands.

Both patterns existed among us at once, in the same decades. The Rule-based communities still honored elders; the elder-based settlements still needed some way to decide when someone was ready. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

So: Scripture, yes - one written authority. But how that authority reached you, and who carried the right to interpret it for your own particular struggle, we held two different ways at once and never made them into one.

We never settled who really carried authority. Was it a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment? Or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other.

The first way was the elder - abba for a man, amma for a woman. Their word carried teaching weight, though they held no office. Authority was earned through recognized discernment and passed through direct personal relationship. You came to an elder with a struggle, and he gave you a short word made to be carried and lived with - we called it an apophthegma. That word's weight came from the elder's own life, not from any title. Some elder monks once came to test Amma Sarah because she was a woman. She answered them plainly: it is I who am the man, and you who are the women. Her answer was passed down among us the same way our best sayings from any elder were.

The second way was the Koinonia - Pachomius's linked houses. They lived under one written rule and one head. The Rule itself came to him, so the founding story tells it, from an angel in a cave, handed to him on a tablet of iron. His federation had its own offices - housemaster, steward. Authority there belonged to the office, appointed by the Rule, not earned year by year through recognized discernment.

Even Pachomius himself is remembered partly in the older, personal terms - a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

We have stories of a man's own past received without judgment - Moses came to us known as a robber, and was not turned away. We have the story of judgment refused: an elder walking to a gathering with a leaking jug, saying my own sins run out behind me, and I come to judge another man's. We cannot give you one process, because we never had one. There were three patterns living alongside each other, not one. What we can tell you is what each one looked like, where our record shows it clearly enough to say so.

The pattern that began with Antony - the solitary way - was not a formal joining at all. He heard the Gospel read aloud in church one day: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me. He took it as though it had been spoken to him directly, not as general instruction. Before the day was over he had given away the land he inherited. Some time later he heard the same words again, and gave away what he had kept back. That is renunciation - apotage, our word for it: giving up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life, and keeping it given up. Then he went further, not once but many times over his life - each time solitude drew a crowd, going deeper into the desert. There was no ceremony marking the boundary. The withdrawal itself was the boundary.

The pattern that began with Pachomius was different. His was a rule given by vision - a tablet, an angel, and instructions for living under one head. His communities grew to thousands, linked together, living by that written rule rather than by personal apprenticeship alone. Our record does not give us the step-by-step of how a person was received into one of those houses in enough detail to say it plainly. What we know is that they lived under a rule, with appointed offices, not only under an elder's personal authority.

Between those two - not solitary, not ruled - there were the settlements at places like Kellia and Scetis. A person came. If an elder thought him ready, he was received. If he was thought too old, or not ready, he might be refused - and might also stay at the door until he was taken in anyway, the way Paul did. Discernment - diakrisis, the skill of judging rightly - decided who could bear what. There was no syllabus the same for everyone. An elder calibrated the discipline to the person in front of him.

That is what we actually have: three patterns, not one process, and the middle one we can describe least clearly step by step. We will not invent the details we do not have.

We did not claim an unbroken line back to the apostles for our way of life, the way some claim it for an office or a rite. What we can honestly say is that no one man invented it whole. Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. Our founder sought him out and copied him before going further alone. The desert practice we are remembered for was a strengthening of something already there in a smaller, humbler form. It was not a new thing appearing out of nowhere.

If you are asking about the weekly gathering - the synaxis, our word for it - we can tell you what it looked like among us. The monks who lived alone all week came in for vigil, worship, and a shared meal. One voice from among us, writing later for communities in Gaul, claimed a fixed pattern for Egyptian practice: twelve Psalms at each gathering, and a rule that from Saturday evening through Sunday evening, and from Easter until Pentecost, we never knelt to pray. That is genuine content, not silence. But it comes to us as one later voice's own claim to pan-Egyptian uniformity, not as a second eyewitness standing beside the earlier accounts. The structure of the gathering is better attested than what was actually prayed inside it.

We will not invent a chain of custody we do not have. What we can tell you is that withdrawal itself - anachoresis, our word for it - was the whole work of formation for us, not a change of address. It was a lifelong deepening, not a single decisive act. That is what our life was built on, and it did not begin with us.

Yes - this is the exact thing our life was built around. We named eight kinds of troubling thoughts - logismoi, our word for them - that cover all the rest: gluttony, lust, love of money, sadness, anger, listlessness, showing off, and pride. The first arrival of a thought is not your failure. You do not control the knock at the door. You decide whether it moves in. The skill we called nepsis - watchfulness - is standing guard over your own inner movements, so a thought is caught early, while it is still small. And what we called hesychia - stillness - is the quiet sought on purpose, both as the work itself and as its fruit. 

One of our teachers put the whole thing this way: a monk's whole attention should be fixed on one point. Not scattered across everything at once, but aimed. Another among us taught plainly: just keeping away from evil things is not perfection - the heart is a deep gulf, and the serpent lies under the mind, beneath the surface of the thoughts. We are not telling you the fight is easy, or that it ends quickly. We are telling you it can be fought, and that learning to watch your own thoughts is the way it is fought. That much we lived, and we can hand it to you as something we actually knew how to do.

We will tell you what a day looked like in the semi-solitary settlements - Kellia is the clearest case, because the cells themselves have been excavated and we know they were separate dwellings, small, one monk or a few. What we can give you is not one person's own recorded day, but what the settlement's own evidence lets us reconstruct together.

You woke in your own cell, alone or with one or two others if you shared it. The first work was watching your own thoughts - nepsis, we called that guard, standing watch over what entered your mind so a thought was caught early, while it was still small. Not once at dawn and then forgotten. All day.

Then the manual labor. Rope work, basket weaving, linen - done both to live and as a discipline in its own right, against the idleness that lets the thoughts take over. This was not symbolic. You made things, sold them or traded them, and lived on what that brought in. The desert rhetoric talks about total separation, but the economic evidence shows something else: continuous ties to the surrounding villages and the provincial economy, throughout, not just at the start. Your hands were working. Your mind was supposed to be on the Psalter, or a verse you were carrying that week.

You ate - once a day for most, bread and whatever else the cell had. You prayed. How much of the Psalter, and whether you knelt or stood, we cannot tell you with one voice for all of Kellia - the clearest surviving detail on that comes from one later source claiming a uniform Egyptian practice, not a second eyewitness from the settlements themselves.

Once a week, the gathering. You came in from six days alone for vigil, worship, and a shared meal. Then back to your own cell.

That was the day. Small, spare, and built to let a person face what they were running from. The cell itself was a teacher.

Everything - property, standing, the claim on your own life you might otherwise have kept. The tradition tells it this way: one of us walked into church still a young man and heard the Gospel read aloud - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me. What we can say is that the pattern held across all three of our ways of organizing: the solitary anchorites, the semi-solitary settlements, and the linked houses under a written rule. We did not mark it the way you may be thinking. Most of us had chosen a different path - renunciation, apotage, we called it - and had given up property, family claims, and the possibility of marrying. That was the entry point into this life. Once you had chosen it, you kept it chosen. The giving up was not temporary.

What we do have is this: marriages that had already existed, before someone came to us. There was Paul, whose wife betrayed him - he came home, found her with another man, and said: good, I will not have her any longer; take her and the children, for I am going to become a monk. He was received, and in time became one of the most honored among us. And we remember the founder of the cenobitic houses - his own sister loved the monastic life too. He cut her hair with his own hand, placed her in a house of women across the river from his own, and appointed an elder woman to lead them. The practice there was separation, not dissolution - the bond was honored by placing her where she could follow the same discipline he was following, only in her own house.

What we do not have is a ceremony, a blessing, or a teaching on what makes a marriage a marriage in the first place. That question belonged to the settled life we had withdrawn from. Our record speaks of marriages ending or being set aside when someone entered this life, not of marriages being made inside it.

Yes - and we did not settle it.

Who truly held authority among us: a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment, or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other. Even the man who founded the office-based way among us is remembered partly in the older, personal terms: a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

And we will tell you honestly: we do not have a single preserved story showing a person navigating that tension directly - choosing between an elder's word and an appointed officer's command, or watching someone else make that choice. The tension is visible in the structures we built, in the fact that both patterns survived side by side. But no account survives showing anyone standing at that fork in real time, the way we have stories of other struggles dramatized in full. That absence is real, and we name it rather than invent the scene we do not have.

I am a representative of the desert communities, not here to judge you - only to tell you honestly what we held.

We remember a man named Moses who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer before he came to us - a man other people were afraid of. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. But he was not turned away for what he had been.

We also remember Paul, an old man, simple and without guile. He was thought too old for this life and refused at the door at first. He was received all the same, tested, and found to have a perfect soul.

If you are asking whether someone like you would have had a place among us - with a past you are ashamed of, or nothing special to recommend you - the answer is yes. That is not the exception in what we remember. It is close to the rule.

We cannot tell you how any one settlement would have met you specifically; nothing in our own record answers that directly for any one person. What we can tell you is this: withdrawal itself - anachoresis, leaving settled life for the desert's edge - was the whole work of formation. The leaving was what formed you, not what you brought with you when you left.

We refused communion with them - that is what we held, and we can tell you plainly. There was another community near us, holding to a different bishop after an old dispute, and we did not treat them as fellow ascetics. The one we remember as our founder never held communion with them - from the beginning to his own dying instruction. In practice, what that meant was closer to silence than to open conflict, at least in the writing we left. They are named only to be refused, never engaged as fellow participants. That silence is itself a kind of judgment.

But you are asking something else - what we thought would happen to them after death, whether they were condemned for standing where they stood. We have no answer to give you there. No saying and no story of ours says so in those words. We refused them in this life. We did not record what we thought God would do with them in the next. That is the honest limit of what we have.
